text: Metformin 500mg. Take one tablet twice daily, with breakfast and with the evening meal. Never take it on an empty stomach. Prescribed by Dr. Patel for type 2 diabetes.
Lisinopril 10mg. Take one tablet each morning, before breakfast. For blood pressure. If a dose is missed, skip it and take the next one at the usual time. Do not double up.
Atorvastatin 20mg. Take one tablet at bedtime. For cholesterol. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking this medicine.
Aspirin 75mg. Take one tablet daily after lunch. Low dose, for heart protection. Take with food to protect the stomach.
Vitamin D 800 IU. One capsule daily with any meal. Recommended year round.
Paracetamol 500mg may be taken as needed for knee pain, up to two tablets at a time and no more than eight tablets in twenty four hours. Leave at least four hours between doses.
Morning medicines, taken before or with breakfast: lisinopril 10mg and metformin 500mg. The blue pill organiser on the kitchen windowsill holds the morning doses.
Evening medicines: metformin 500mg with the evening meal, then atorvastatin 20mg at bedtime. The green organiser holds the evening doses.
Serious allergy to penicillin. It causes a severe rash and swelling. This is his most important allergy.
The penicillin allergy must be mentioned at every medical and dental appointment. It is recorded on the GP file and on the medical bracelet worn on his left wrist.
Mild allergy to shellfish. Causes an itchy rash but no breathing difficulty. Avoid prawns, crab and mussels.
History of two falls in the past year, both in the bathroom. Grab rails were fitted in March. Always use the walking stick on stairs and outdoors.
Moderate hearing loss in the right ear. He wears a hearing aid in the left ear only. Speak clearly and from his left side.
The hearing aid batteries are changed on the first Sunday of each month. Spares are kept in the kitchen drawer.
Cardiology appointment with Dr. Patel on Tuesday the fifteenth of September at half past two in the afternoon, at Riverside Clinic, second floor.
Sarah is driving him to the cardiology appointment on the fifteenth of September and will arrive to collect him at a quarter to two.
GP medication review with Dr. Okafor on Thursday the twenty fourth of September at ten fifteen in the morning at Hollybank Surgery. Bring all current pill boxes to the appointment.
Dental check up on Monday the fifth of October at eleven in the morning with Mr. Reeves.
Blood test at Hollybank Surgery on Wednesday the seventh of October at eight forty in the morning. Fasting is required, so no breakfast beforehand, but water and morning medicines are fine.
Physiotherapy for the left knee, every second Friday at nine thirty in the morning at Riverside Clinic. The next session is Friday the eighteenth of September.
Chiropody visit at home on the last Wednesday of each month at two in the afternoon. Margaret comes to the house, so no travel is needed.
Sarah is his daughter and his main emergency contact. Her mobile number is 07700 900 118.
Sarah lives about twenty minutes away in Ashford and visits on Sundays, usually early afternoon, often bringing Amara.
Michael is the son. He lives in Manchester and telephones on Wednesday evenings. His mobile number is 07700 900 224.
Hollybank Surgery is the GP practice. The telephone number is 01233 555 040. Dr. Okafor is the named doctor. The surgery is open from eight in the morning until six in the evening on weekdays.
Joan next door at number fourteen has a spare key and can help in an emergency. Her number is 01233 555 761. She is usually at home in the mornings.
His name is William Hartley, but everyone calls him Bill. He dislikes being called William, which he says sounds like he is in trouble.
His wife Margaret died three years ago in April. They were married for fifty one years. He likes talking about her, particularly about their garden and their holidays in Whitby.
He has three grandchildren. Ellie is nineteen and studying veterinary science in Bristol. Tom is fifteen and plays cricket. Amara is seven and is learning the recorder, loudly.
He worked for thirty eight years as a railway signalman, mostly on the Kent coast line. He is proud of it and enjoys explaining how signal boxes worked.
The garden matters a great deal to him. He grows tomatoes, runner beans and dahlias. The dahlias were Margaret's favourite. He walks out to look at them after breakfast most mornings.
He follows cricket closely and supports Kent. He listens to Test Match Special on the radio and will happily talk about it for as long as anyone lets him.
He wakes around half past six, has tea and toast, takes his morning medicines, then walks around the garden. He listens to the radio news at eight.
He has his evening meal around six, watches the news, then reads or listens to the radio. He goes to bed around ten, after his bedtime tablet.
He prefers tea to coffee, strong with a little milk. He does not like being fussed over or spoken to slowly. He would rather be asked than told.
He is comfortable with the radio and the television but finds smartphones frustrating. He would rather speak to someone than type. He does not use email.
He walks well indoors but uses a stick outdoors and on stairs. He can manage the stairs alone but prefers company. He should not carry anything heavy up or down.
He makes his own breakfast and lunch. A hot meal is delivered on weekdays at around midday. Sarah cooks on Sundays. He should eat before taking metformin.
In an emergency, call 999 first, then call Sarah on 07700 900 118.
He wears a pendant alarm during the day and keeps it on the bedside table at night. To call for help, press and hold its button for three seconds.
Sarah should be told the same day about any fall, any chest pain, any new confusion, or if medicines are missed for more than one day. Routine matters can wait for the Sunday visit.
